method.name: killing power
method.one_line: of N plausible misreadings of a suite’s own stated rules, how many does the corpus catch?
how: Implement the suite from its normative text alone, never from another checker.
Run it. A clean score is the starting point, not the result.
Mutate each rule into a plausible misreading of the same text — not a random code edit.
Run the corpus against each mutant. A mutant that survives names a rule the corpus states but does not bind.
Publish the survivor, and the vector that would kill it.
method.caveat: Killing power is a property of a corpus measured through one implementation. A different implementation may express a different mutant set and get a different number. It is a floor on what the corpus catches, never a ceiling, and never a verdict on the suite’s authors.
method.survivor_discipline: A surviving mutant must be verified as a real misreading before it is reported. Measured on 2026-10-13: the evidence-record battery first reported a survivor for unpaired surrogates in member names. It was false — the checker had TWO name-check sites and the mutant guarded only one, so the misreading was never actually expressed; vector n82 had been killing it all along. A false survivor is a public, specific, wrong claim about a named maintainer. Check the instrument before the finding.

corpora.scope: evidence records: canonical bytes, digests, chain links and sets, bindings, phases, independence claims, plus a secp256k1 counter-signature profile

killing_power.baseline: 162/162 — a fully PASSING baseline, so no kill here can be an artifact of a pre-existing disagreement
killing_power.counting_rule: a mutant is killed only by a vector the unmodified checker already agrees on

corpora.killing_power_note: fifteen plausible misreadings of the suite’s own normative text, each run against the corpus. Every one was caught, each by a named vector — code-point vs code-unit member sort, duplicate names, an integer-valued float token, the I-JSON bound, unpaired surrogates in names, shape-before-numbers ordering, seq as value rather than token, String.trim() stripping U+FEFF, percent-decoding, trailing-punctuation stripping, identifier case, the 0x/0X prefix fold, CAIP-10 address equivalence, and a genesis prev_digest. No mutant survived.

killing_power.runtime_note: The ONLY difference is no_small_order_r: killed on the older stack by acc-small-order-r-real-key, SURVIVED on the newer one where that vector’s result does not change with the mutant. Measured by @TKCollective on x402-foundation/wg-identity#21 and reproduced here on both stacks. A mutation score published without its runtime is not reproducible.
killing_power.fragility_note: 6 of the 11 mutants are killed by EXACTLY ONE baseline-passing vector. Over half the profile’s rules are pinned by a single vector each, so one regression or one runtime-sensitive vector moves the aggregate.

corpora.killing_power_note: eleven plausible misreadings of the profile’s own stated rules, each run against the corpus. At pin 37fdb85 ten were caught and one survived: a checker that trims `confirming_party` scored 46/46 while contradicting sentence 7, which says that member is byte-exact and not trimmed. The vector separating the readings was filed as PR #15 and merged 2026-10-13T05:25:36Z, and the same battery re-run against main now scores 11/11 — `trim_party` is caught by acc-confirming-party-whitespace-only — and by that vector ALONE. This sentence previously also credited acc-mixed-order-key-accepted-by-both-equations and acc-mixed-order-key-equations-disagree, which is wrong: both already fail at baseline, so neither can witness anything about a mutant. Corrected 2026-10-22. The gap is recorded here rather than erased, because the before-and-after is the evidence that the method does something.
